system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2186-04-11 18:00:00 to 2186-04-13 09:26:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with mitochondrial disease, autonomic dysfunction, coronary artery disease, and hypogammaglobulinemia was admitted for observation during a scheduled biweekly IVIG infusion. He reported a brief episode of near-syncope at home triggered by cold exposure, but was asymptomatic on admission. The IVIG infusion was administered with premedication and IV fluids. During the infusion, he developed mild chest tightness, shortness of breath, and hand tingling, which improved with oxygen and slowing the infusion rate. Symptoms resolved post-infusion, and he remained hemodynamically stable without hypoxia or arrhythmias. He was monitored on telemetry and observed overnight. No medication changes were made. He was discharged home in stable condition with plans to continue outpatient IVIG and follow-up with specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospitalists. You're here today for your scheduled IVIG infusion, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. Every two weeks, I come in for the IVIG. This time, though, I wanted to do it slowly overnight because I’m really sensitive to fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your history mentions you're very fluid-sensitive due to your mitochondrial disease and orthostatic hypotension. We’ll make sure the infusion is slow and monitored closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Last time, I got chest tightness and shortness of breath when it ran too fast. They slowed it down and gave me oxygen, and it got better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I reviewed your last admission. You also had some tingling in your hands. We’ll pre-medicate you with Benadryl and start with IV fluids to help prevent a reaction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. I’ve had trouble with different IVIG formulations too. This current one seems to be working best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. We’ll continue with the same formulation. Your labs were drawn earlier—your IgG level was 813, which is within the target range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. I’ve been having fewer infections since starting IVIG—no pneumonia or cellulitis in months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we hope for. IVIG is helping your immune system stay strong. We’ll keep you on telemetry tonight to monitor your heart rhythm, given your history of supraventricular tachycardia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My heart can act up, but my EKGs are usually normal, even when I feel funny.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your physical exam today is stable—blood pressure 158 over 98, lungs clear, heart regular. We’ll start your IV fluids now, then begin the IVIG infusion in about 30 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also get groggy after the infusion. Last time, I didn’t feel safe driving home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll plan for you to stay overnight then. You can go home tomorrow morning once you’re feeling clear-headed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’ve got family picking me up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started the IVIG at a low rate. You’re on 2 liters of oxygen by nasal cannula as a precaution, and we’re monitoring your vitals every hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel okay so far. Just a little warm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nurse mentioned you had mild chest discomfort a few minutes ago. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s still there—kind of a pressure, not sharp. And I’m a bit short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get an EKG right away. Given your cardiac history, we want to be cautious, but these symptoms are common with IVIG reactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EKG shows normal sinus rhythm, no ischemia. We’ll keep you on oxygen and slow the IVIG rate further. Does that sound okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. I’d rather go slow than feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve tolerated the rest of the infusion well. We’re finishing up now. Any chest pressure or breathing issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. The chest pressure is gone. Still a bit tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. We’re giving you an additional 500 cc bolus of normal saline after the infusion to help with volume balance, since you’re prone to orthostatic hypotension.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I usually need that after IVIG. Helps me not feel dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling? Any residual symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning. I’m awake, but still groggy. My head feels heavy. I definitely wouldn’t want to drive yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. We’ll keep you here for a few more hours to make sure you’re alert enough to go home safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. Is my blood pressure okay? I know it was high last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s 158 over 88 this morning—still a bit elevated, but stable. We’ll continue your home meds, including valsartan and metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my GERD has been quiet. Still taking the esomeprazole at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep you on that. All your other medications are unchanged—atorvastatin, clopidogrel, ranolazine. We did switch your aspirin to a chewable 81 mg tablet once daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a small adjustment—chewable aspirin is easier on the stomach and still effective for your heart protection. You were on 162 mg twice daily, but current guidelines support 81 mg daily for long-term use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re looking more alert now. Vital signs are stable—heart rate 68, oxygen 96% on room air. I think you’re ready to go home this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. This was the last planned inpatient IVIG, right? They’re hoping to switch me to outpatient eventually?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, this is the final inpatient admission for IVIG. If your reactions continue to be mild and manageable, the team may consider outpatient infusion with close monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like that. Fewer hospital stays would be nice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll coordinate with your immunology team. For now, keep taking all your meds as prescribed and follow up with your specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Someone will be by shortly to review everything with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning again. You’re officially discharged. Your condition is stable, and you’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning. I feel much better—clear-headed and ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Remember to continue all your medications, especially the new chewable aspirin. Follow up with your cardiologist and immunologist as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And if I have another reaction during IVIG, should I come back here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially if you have chest pressure, trouble breathing, or dizziness. But with the slower rate and pre-meds, we expect fewer issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we hope you continue to do well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best. Have a good day.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with hypogammaglobulinemia, mitochondrial myopathy, coronary artery disease, and orthostatic hypotension was admitted for scheduled inpatient IVIG infusion. He received premedication with IV fluids and Benadryl, and the infusion was administered slowly overnight due to his fluid sensitivity. During the infusion, he experienced mild chest discomfort and shortness of breath, which resolved with oxygen and rate reduction. He remained on telemetry and was observed overnight. The following day, he reported residual grogginess but improved mental clarity by afternoon. He was discharged home in stable condition with medication adjustments, including a switch to chewable aspirin, and plans for potential transition to outpatient IVIG. No acute complications occurred.
